When every signal is loud, people learn to ignore all of them, and the one that matters gets missed. Fewer, better-grouped alerts get more attention, not less.
Group related signals into one alert with a count. Rate-limit repeats. Reserve red, sound and motion for things a person must act on now. Normal stays quiet.
Group alerts that share a cause; show the count, not 23 toasts.
Only critical can animate, and only gently.
Normal status gets no colour fill and no badge in lists.
Five charts take minutes to read; one score with a clear band takes a second. Showing the factors beside it keeps the number trustworthy.
Combine weak signals into a health score with clear bands, and keep the breakdown one click away. A score without its factors is a black box people stop trusting.
Show the score, its band, and the biggest factor together.
Use the same bands everywhere for the same entity type.
Each metric shows the threshold it’s judged against.
Most bad values are typos or misjudged defaults, not intent. A warning catches the first kind; a block stops the dangerous kind.
Inputs that matter get two limits. Past the soft limit, warn and ask for a reason that lands on the timeline. Past the hard limit, block and say the maximum.
Show the usual range before anyone types.
The reason for a soft override is recorded.
Risky actions fail on things everyone knew but nobody checked. A short, specific checklist at the moment of action catches them in seconds.
Before a risky action, show three to five checks that a person can verify in seconds. Pre-fill what the system already knows. The action button unlocks when every item is checked.
Three to five items, phrased as facts.
Show evidence: who approved and when.
The button names the action; the toast repeats it.
Wrong-target mistakes happen when two things look alike: prod and staging, orders-eu and orders-us. Reading the exact name breaks autopilot.
Before deleting or overwriting, the person types the exact name and sees the environment badge beside it. Wrong-environment mistakes become hard to make.
PROD badge sits next to the name, not in a corner.
During an incident the first question is always “what changed?”. One ordered record answers it without hunting across tools.
Every entity has one ordered record of alerts, changes, deploys, notes and who did them. Nobody hunts across five tabs during an incident.
Group by day; show who and when.
Soft-limit justifications and pause-point completions are recorded here.
Link alerts to the change that preceded them.
Overview screens are glanced at, often from across a room. If the problem isn’t obvious in two seconds, the screen hasn’t done its job.
Overviews have a station density with large numerals for wall displays. Tiles sort worst first, so the top-left is always the one to look at.
Station density scales type, spacing and numerals together.
Severity is readable in greyscale, from a distance.
